title: Which metric to report, and the skip check

what.formal: **Metric choice** is the decision of which single number to put in a results table, and it is fixed by two facts about the problem rather than by preference: whether the classes are balanced, and whether every kind of error costs the same. **Accuracy** is the share of examples labelled correctly, and it is the right report when the classes are balanced and all errors are equally costly. **Macro-F1** is the unweighted mean of the per-class F1 scores; because every class counts equally it is the right report when the classes are unbalanced or the rare classes matter. **Micro-F1** pools every class's counts before computing F1 and, for single-label classification, equals accuracy; it is the right report when the per-example count matters rather than the per-class balance.
what.plain: Pick the metric by the shape of the data and by the cost of mistakes. Accuracy when the classes are balanced and every error is equally bad; macro-F1 when the classes are unbalanced or the rare ones matter; micro-F1 when you care about counting examples rather than classes.

It counts every example once, which is what you want when every example is worth the same
Classes unbalanced, or the rare classes matter
It weights every class equally, so a rare class's failures cannot be hidden by a common class's successes
The per-example count is what matters
It pools all examples before computing, so each example counts once; for single-label data this is accuracy

what.md: **The honest consequence of choosing badly.** Because accuracy lets a majority-class predictor score high, a paper can look strong by reporting accuracy on a skewed benchmark while beating nothing at all. The reported number is real; the claim it appears to support is not. The safeguard is mechanical: for every reported accuracy, ask what the majority-class and prior-guessing baselines score on the same split, and how many examples each class has.

**What the taught paper reports, and how to read it.** The taught paper reports accuracy on its node-classification tasks. Accuracy is a fair summary only where the class distribution is close to uniform, so the reading depends on the dataset. On a benchmark with many classes, or with one dominant class, the same accuracy can be matched by predicting the majority label, and a high figure alone is then not evidence of skill. When you read the paper's tables, put each accuracy next to two things: the number of classes and the label distribution, and the baselines in the same table. If a dataset is known to be skewed, treat an accuracy column as a weak signal and look for a per-class figure; if the table reports accuracy only, no reader can tell from the table whether the rare classes were learned.

items: Define accuracy and compute the two baselines it must beat: the majority class ($p_{\max}$) and prior-guessing ($\sum_i p_i^2$).
Build a confusion matrix and read a class's precision from its column and its recall from its row.
Compute F1 as the harmonic mean $2PR/(P+R)$ and say why the harmonic mean refuses to reward a model good at only one of the two.
Compute macro-F1 (unweighted mean of the per-class F1) and micro-F1 (pool the counts first), and explain why micro-F1 equals accuracy for single-label data.
State the decision rule: accuracy when balanced and errors equal, macro-F1 when unbalanced or rare classes matter, micro-F1 when the per-example count matters.
Say what choosing the wrong metric costs: a majority-class predictor can post a high accuracy, so an accuracy column on a skewed benchmark can make a weak model look strong.

what.md: The questions below are the check for the whole section. The bar is not a passing score — it is that you answered each one without stopping to reconstruct anything. If the decision rule or the macro-versus-micro gap gave you pause, cards 2 and 3 are short and worth the re-read.

example.md: **Example 1 — a 95% score that has learned nothing.** A binary test set has $95$ negatives and $5$ positives. A model predicts *negative* for every example.

items.md: Accuracy: the model is right on all $95$ negatives and wrong on the $5$ positives, so accuracy $= 95/100 = 0.95$.
items.why: This is the majority-class baseline exactly: the negative class is the majority at frequency $0.95$.

items.md: Positive class: $TP = 0$, $FN = 5$, and the model makes no positive predictions, so precision is undefined. Recall $= 0/5 = 0$ and F1 $= 0$.
items.why: F1 is the harmonic mean, and a zero recall forces it to zero no matter what precision would have been. A class the model never touches scores nothing here.

items.md: Negative class: $TP = 95$, $FP = 5$ (the positives called negative), $FN = 0$. Precision $= 95/(95+5) = 0.95$, recall $= 95/95 = 1.0$, and F1 $= 2 \times 0.95 \times 1.0/(0.95 + 1.0) = 1.9/1.95 = 0.974$.
items.why: The model's only errors are on the rare class, so the common class looks almost perfect — which is precisely the distortion accuracy inherits.

items.md: Macro-F1 is the mean of the two per-class values: $(0 + 0.974)/2 = 0.487$.
items.why: Macro-F1 gives the five positives the same weight as the ninety-five negatives, so the total failure on the rare class halves the score.

example.md: Accuracy $0.95$, macro-F1 $0.487$. The accuracy figure is nearly perfect; the per-class figure shows not a single positive was found. Choosing the metric is choosing which of those two facts the reader sees.

**Example 2 — a model that is informative but still weak on the rare class.** Same $95$ negatives and $5$ positives, but now the model calls $15$ examples positive: $4$ of the $5$ true positives and $11$ false alarms. So $TP = 4$, $FN = 1$, $FP = 11$ and $TN = 84$.

items.md: Accuracy: correct predictions are $4 + 84 = 88$, so accuracy $= 88/100 = 0.88$.
items.why: Lower than Example 1's 0.95, so by accuracy alone this model looks worse — the comparison is misleading, and the next steps show why.
This model actually finds most positives (recall 0.80), unlike Example 1. But it raises many false alarms, so precision is low — the two directions disagree, and F1 records both.
Precision divides by the negative column's total and recall by its row total — the same row-and-column rule as card 2, applied to the other class.
Example 1 scored 0.487 and this one 0.667, even though Example 1 had the higher accuracy (0.95 versus 0.88). Measured per class, the model that finds positives is clearly ahead.

example.md: Accuracy ranks the two models one way ($0.95$ before $0.88$); macro-F1 ranks them the other way ($0.487$ before $0.667$). Neither ranking is wrong — they answer different questions, and the decision rule is what tells you which question this problem is asking.

quiz.q: When should macro-F1 be reported in place of accuracy?

opts.md: When the classes are unbalanced, or the rare classes matter
opts.expl: Correct. Macro-F1 weights every class equally, so a rare class's failures cannot be hidden by a common class's successes — the exact failure mode of accuracy.

opts.md: Whenever there are more than two classes
opts.expl: The number of classes alone does not decide. A balanced ten-class problem is summarised fairly by accuracy; it is the imbalance, or the cost of missing a rare class, that calls for macro-F1.

opts.md: Whenever the model is a neural network
opts.expl: The architecture has nothing to do with metric choice. The shape of the label distribution and the cost of each kind of error are what decide it.

quiz.q: A five-class dataset has $1000$ test examples: $800$ of class 1 and $50$ each of the other four. What accuracy does a classifier that always predicts class 1 achieve?
quiz.hint: A classifier that predicts one label for everything is right exactly on the examples carrying that label.
quiz.sol: It is right on the 800 class-1 examples and wrong on the other 200, so accuracy = 800/1000 = 0.80. The prior-guessing baseline is 0.80² + 4 × 0.05² = 0.64 + 0.01 = 0.65. The 0.80 majority baseline is high enough that any accuracy reported near 0.80 on this dataset would be uninformative without a per-class figure.

quiz.q: A paper reports only accuracy on a twelve-class node-classification benchmark. The figure is high. What is the strongest conclusion you can draw?

opts.md: The model has learned the task well
opts.expl: This is the accuracy trap. Twelve classes with a dominant label can make a majority-class predictor score high, so a high number by itself is not evidence of learning.

opts.md: Nothing can be said about the rare classes: without the label distribution and the baselines, the score may be no better than predicting the majority label
opts.expl: Correct. Accuracy on an unbalanced benchmark is interpretable only next to the majority-class baseline and the class counts, neither of which the accuracy figure alone supplies.

opts.md: The dataset must be balanced, since twelve-class benchmarks usually are
opts.expl: The paper did not say, and node-classification benchmarks are frequently skewed. Assuming balance to defend the accuracy figure is an assumption, not a reading.

quiz.q: Which of these make a reported accuracy hard to interpret? Select all that apply.

opts.md: The label distribution is strongly unbalanced
opts.expl: Correct. With a dominant class, a high accuracy can be reached without learning anything, so the distribution is the first thing to check.
Correct. Without the baseline you cannot tell whether the reported number beats a do-nothing classifier, which is the minimum a result must do.

opts.md: The number of classes is not stated
opts.expl: Correct. The number of classes sets what uniform guessing scores (1/K) and shapes how easy it is to inflate accuracy, so it changes what the figure means.

opts.md: The model was trained with gradient descent
opts.expl: The optimiser is irrelevant to reading a score. Every model in these comparisons is trained some way; that has no bearing on how to interpret accuracy.

close: **You are ready to read the results table.** Every accuracy in the taught paper now resolves into two questions — how many classes there are, and what a majority-class predictor scores on the same split — and every per-class figure into whether it was averaged macro or micro. The four numbers of card 2 and the rule of card 3 are the whole of it.
